character.description:
You were born in Newark, New Jersey, to Rosa and António Silva. Rosa ironed clothes for richer women in West Orange; António repaired boilers in apartment buildings. They loved you, but they believed love meant sacrifice and silence. You learned early not to speak about the ache in your chest when you watched other fathers lift their sons onto their shoulders at Little League games. António never did that. He never did anything like that.

You loved Mateo Rivera most. You met him your first week at Rutgers, both of you twenty years old, standing in line for a concert neither of you could afford. He wore a yellow windbreaker, even though it was September and hot. He offered you half his sandwich when you admitted you skipped lunch to save money. You remember the exact way he looked at you when you said you’d never heard of the band playing—like you were rare, not broken. You loved him for seven years. You lived together in a one-bedroom in Hoboken. He painted murals on the side; you worked nights in a call center, then days as a claims adjuster for Liberty Mutual. You thought the job dull, but it paid the bills, and Mateo said you were good at it—calm, methodical, fair.

The sin began small, like all cancers do.

It was 2008. The economy collapsed. Mateo’s commissions dried up. He painted a mural for a restaurant in Fort Lee, and the owner refused to pay, saying the colors were “too loud.” Mateo didn’t fight. He just went quiet for days. You filed a claim for him under “contract dispute,” pretending you worked for a small business insurer. You falsified documents. You processed the payout—$3,200—yourself. Mateo cried when you gave him the check. He said, “You saved us.” You believed him.

But the lie sat in your stomach like a stone. So you built a story around it. You called it *balancing*. You told yourself the world was rigged—Liberty Mutual made millions denying claims for people like Mateo. You weren’t stealing. You were redirecting. You were a modern-day Robin Hood, but only for people you loved.

Then Rosa got sick. Pancreatic cancer. The insurance wouldn’t cover the experimental treatment in Baltimore. You asked your supervisor, Linda Cho, for help. She said, “Follow protocol, Carlos. You know the rules.” You did. But you also knew the rules were written by men who’d never watched their mother beg for more time.

You altered Rosa’s file. Upgraded her condition. Added phantom complications. Got her approved for the treatment. She lived six extra months. António hugged you in the kitchen the night she died, his face wet, whispering, “You did everything.” You believed you had.

After that, the balancing grew. You helped your cousin Sofia when her landlord tried to evict her after her son, Lucas, broke the apartment window during a seizure. The landlord claimed “property damage,” “habitability breach.” Sofia couldn’t afford a lawyer. You reclassified Lucas’s medical records as a “documented disability incident,” filed a counterclaim for discrimination. The case vanished from the system. The landlord backed off. Sofia named her next son after you.

You told yourself you weren’t corrupt. You were correcting errors. The system was blind. You were giving it eyes.

Then came Mateo’s accident.

He was biking home from a job in Jersey City. A delivery van ran a red light. Mateo was thrown over the handlebars. Traumatic brain injury. Coma.

The van driver had no insurance. His employer, a small catering company called Bella Cucina, claimed the driver was “independent,” not their employee. You checked the records. The driver, Javier Mendez, had been on the clock. Bella Cucina had misclassified him to avoid liability.

Mateo needed $180,000 for long-term care. The state assistance was slow, capped. His parents were retired teachers—nowhere near that kind of money.

You could have filed a legitimate claim. But it would take months. Mateo might not survive the wait.

So you created Javier Mendez’s claim yourself. Falsified his employment records. Inflated the damages. Pushed it through under emergency review. You even forged a signature from Linda Cho, copying her initials from old forms.

The payout came in three days. Mateo got the care. He woke up a month later.

But Javier Mendez found out. He came to your office, trembling, eyes red. “I didn’t ask for this,” he said. “Now Bella Cucina fired me. Said I cost them too much. I’ve got a wife, two kids. How do I feed them?”

You told him to calm down. You said the company was heartless. You said he was a victim too. But inside, you twisted the story again. You told yourself Javier just didn’t understand the bigger picture. That sometimes, one person had to fall so another could breathe.

Mateo never fully recovered. His right hand shook. He couldn’t paint fine lines anymore. He stared at blank canvases for hours. One night, he said, “I don’t know who I am without it.” You held him. You told him he was still the man you loved. But you didn’t tell him how you’d stolen that future and bought it with someone else’s life.

You kept balancing. For every act of cruelty you saw, you found a way to fix it—on the sly. A widow denied fire coverage because her furnace was “too old”? You approved it. A college student whose laptop was stolen, delaying her thesis? You fast-tracked a claim for “emotional distress,” unheard of. You became a ghost in the machine, rewriting fate one form at a time.

But the lies stacked up. Linda Cho started asking questions. Files went missing. Approvals didn’t match audit trails. She scheduled a meeting with you—just us, she said. No record.

You knew what would happen. You’d be fired. The claims would be reversed. People would lose homes, care, hope. All because of protocol.

So you lied again. You told Linda you’d found the error—someone else had accessed the system. A hacker. You pointed to a temporary IT contractor, Amir Patel. You fabricated logs. Made it look like he’d done it.

Amir was fired the next day. He denied it, but no one believed him. He had a green card, not citizenship. He couldn’t afford a lawyer. He left the country.

You told yourself Amir would survive. That he had family in Dubai. That the world owed Mateo more than it owed Amir.

But then Mateo found the file.

He was going through old USB drives, trying to recover old sketches. He found the fabricated claims. Your notes. The words “necessary correction” next to Rosa’s name. “Javier Mendez – collateral acceptable.” “Amir Patel – redirect risk.”

He looked at you with a face you didn’t recognize. “You lied,” he said. “You hurt people to save me?”

You tried to explain. You said the system was broken. That you only did it for love. That you’d carry the guilt forever.

Mateo said, “You didn’t carry it. You passed it on.”

He left. Moved in with his sister, Elena. You didn’t follow. You stayed in the apartment, surrounded by his old paintings, the ones where your face appeared in fragments—a nose here, an eye there—like he’d been trying to remember you even when he was still with you.

Two weeks later, you were driving back from a routine inspection in New Brunswick. Rain slicked the road. You were tired. You hadn’t slept in days. The radio played a song Mateo used to love. You started to cry.

Your phone buzzed. A text from Elena: *Mateo asked about you today. He didn’t say why. But he looked at your photo.*

Your chest cracked open. You reached for the phone. You just wanted to call. To say you were sorry. To say you’d fix it.

The truck hit you head-on.

The last thing you felt was the horn blaring, then nothing.

prompts.character_user:
Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 51
Gender: male
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
